name: HTTP/2 Connection Multiplexing
tagline: Multiplexing concurrent binary streams over a single TCP connection with HPACK header compression and flow control, eliminating HTTP/1.1 HoL blocking.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of HTTP/2—from binary frame streams and HPACK dynamic tables to TCP-level head-of-line blocking, L4 pinning, and CVE-2023-44487 Rapid Reset.

spark.summary: HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) multiplexes concurrent binary request/response streams over a single TCP connection using HPACK header compression and flow control, eliminating HTTP/1.1 application-layer head-of-line blocking.
spark.keyTakeaway: When nodes partition or reboot past retry windows, HTTP/2 removes the 6-connection-per-origin browser limit and HTTP/1.1 pipelining stalls, but all streams still share one TCP congestion window—so packet loss above ~1–2% causes TCP-level head-of-line blocking that only HTTP/3 (QUIC) solves.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** HTTP/1.1 forces browsers to open 6 parallel TCP connections per origin (each paying TCP + TLS handshakes and cold slow-start) and still stalls behind slow responses.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Interleaved HTTP/2 Frames on 1 TCP Connection (vs. TCP Packet Loss) (Client (1 TCP) -> TCP Congestion Win -> Origin / Envoy); Mobile HTTP/3 (QUIC) -> Edge CDN -> Internal HTTP/2 L7 Envoy Mesh (Mobile Client -> Edge CDN / ALB -> Envoy L7 Mesh -> Backend Pods).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Compare the three HTTP generations across multiplexing, HoL blocking, and proxy support. Modern platforms terminate **HTTP/3 (QUIC)** and **HTTP/2** at the CDN/edge (protecting mobile users from packet-loss HoL stalls) and route **HTTP/2** internally through **L7 Envoy sidecars** for per-stream load balancing.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore how HTTP/2 interacts with L7 load balancing, keep-alive timeouts, and TLS handshake storms.

learningJourney.title: What is HTTP/2 Binary Framing & Multiplexing

explanation.foundation: HTTP/1.1 forces browsers to open 6 parallel TCP connections per origin (each paying TCP + TLS handshakes and cold slow-start) and still stalls behind slow responses. **HTTP/2 (RFC 9113)** splits every message into binary frames (`HEADERS`, `DATA`, `SETTINGS`, `WINDOW_UPDATE`, `RST_STREAM`, `GOAWAY`) tagged with a 31-bit **Stream ID**.
explanation.core: Dozens of concurrent streams (`SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS = 100–256`) interleave on **one** warmed TCP connection, while **HPACK (RFC 7541)** compresses repeated headers/cookies by ~80% using a static table, a 4,096-byte dynamic table, and Huffman coding.
explanation.deepDive: In production deployments of HTTP/2 Connection Multiplexing, watch how what is http/2 binary framing & multiplexing interacts with tail latency, retry amplification, and partial failures. decisionFramework.problem: How to implement HTTP/2 Connection Multiplexing without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: When nodes partition or reboot past retry windows, HTTP/2 removes the 6-connection-per-origin browser limit and HTTP/1.1 pipelining stalls, but all streams still share one TCP congestion window—so packet loss above ~1–2% causes TCP-level head-of-line blocking that only HTTP/3 (QUIC) solves.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

options.label: Increase retry counts and remove client timeouts so every request eventually succeeds.

options.explanation: Bounding retries and isolating slow paths preserves healthy capacity and keeps tail latency predictable.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Broadband CDN & Internal gRPC Meshes
benefits: Zero connection-pool churn, 80% smaller headers via HPACK, and 100+ concurrent RPCs per socket.
costs: Requires L7-aware load balancers (Envoy/ALB/Nginx) to balance per-stream instead of per-connection.

comparison.choice: Prefer HTTP/3 (QUIC): Lossy Cellular Networks (>2% Loss)
benefits: QUIC runs over UDP with independent per-stream recovery, eliminating TCP head-of-line blocking.
costs: Higher UDP CPU overhead and occasional enterprise firewall UDP/443 blocking (fallback to H2).

benefits: L7 proxies demultiplex streams evenly across newly scaled backend pods.
costs: L4 VIPs pin all multiplexed streams on one TCP socket to a single backend pod.

learningJourney.markdownContent:
```yaml
# Envoy HTTP/2 upstream/downstream protocol tuning
typed_extension_protocol_options:
  envoy.extensions.upstreams.http.v3.HttpProtocolOptions:
    "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.upstreams.http.v3.HttpProtocolOptions
    explicit_http_config:
      http2_protocol_options:
        max_concurrent_streams: 128
        initial_stream_window_size: 1048576      # 1 MiB per stream (vs 64 KiB default)
        initial_connection_window_size: 16777216 # 16 MiB per connection
```

advanced.keyTakeaway: When nodes partition or reboot past retry windows, HTTP/2 removes the 6-connection-per-origin browser limit and HTTP/1.1 pipelining stalls, but all streams still share one TCP congestion window—so packet loss above ~1–2% causes TCP-level head-of-line blocking that only HTTP/3 (QUIC) solves.
